title: RTX Wins $22.9 Billion Tomahawk Missile Contract as Pentagon Races to Rebuild Stockpiles
excerpt: The seven-year deal will scale Raytheon's annual Tomahawk production from roughly 60 to more than 1,000 missiles, the largest single munitions contract in years.
body:
• The U.S. Navy awarded RTX unit Raytheon a $22.9 billion, seven-year contract to dramatically increase Tomahawk cruise missile production to more than 1,000 units per year.
  • RTX has already tripled Tomahawk output in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period last year, following a February framework agreement with the Pentagon.
  • The Navy fired more than 850 Tomahawks in the first month of the Iran conflict alone, depleting a pre-war inventory of roughly 3,100 missiles.
  • The deal follows similar multi-year production agreements with Lockheed Martin for THAAD and Patriot interceptors as the Pentagon overhauls its munitions industrial base.

The U.S. Navy on Monday awarded RTX's Raytheon unit a $22.9 billion contract to accelerate production of Tomahawk cruise missiles, the largest single munitions deal in years and a signal that Washington is moving aggressively to rebuild weapons stockpiles drawn down during the Iran conflict and arms transfers to allies.

Under the seven-year agreement, Raytheon will scale annual Tomahawk production from roughly 60 missiles per year to more than 1,000, a roughly sixteenfold increase that will require expanded manufacturing facilities, a larger workforce, and a strengthened supply chain, according to the company.

A Wartime Imperative

The contract reflects the urgency of a military that has burned through precision-guided munitions at a pace few anticipated. The Navy fired more than 850 Tomahawks during the first month of the Iran war alone, according to the Washington Post, consuming more than a quarter of a pre-war inventory that the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated at approximately 3,100 missiles.

"This landmark $22.9 billion investment will accelerate Tomahawk missile delivery to our warfighters at unprecedented speed."

— Hung Cao, Acting Secretary of the Navy

The Navy's fiscal 2027 budget request called for $3 billion to replenish Tomahawk stocks — enough for 785 missiles — a dramatic escalation from the $257 million Congress allocated last year, which funded just 58 units.

Production Already Ramping

Monday's contract formalizes and expands a February framework agreement between RTX and the Pentagon. Raytheon said it has already produced three times as many Tomahawks in the first half of 2026 as it did in the same period last year.

"Tomahawk is the Navy's most important strike weapon, able to target hostile forces hundreds of miles away without ever risking the lives of our sailors," said Raytheon President Phil Jasper. "We are making significant investments in our workforce, technology, supply chain and facilities to dramatically boost production capacity and meet surging demand."

The multi-year structure of the contract is designed to give RTX the confidence to invest billions in new capacity without the risk that the government might scale back orders after the immediate crisis passes — a concern that has historically slowed defense industrial expansion.

Defense Sector Implications

The Tomahawk deal is the latest in a series of massive production agreements the Pentagon has struck with major defense contractors. Lockheed Martin signed similar seven-year contracts earlier this year to quadruple THAAD interceptor production to 400 units annually and boost Patriot PAC-3 output to 2,000 per year. Raytheon itself has separate framework agreements to increase production of AMRAAM air-to-air missiles to at least 1,900 annually and to ramp SM-3 ballistic missile interceptors.

RTX stock rose in early trading Monday before reversing to close down 0.6%. The muted reaction may reflect the fact that investors had already priced in the contract following the February framework announcement.

Undersecretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey framed the deal in broader strategic terms. "The Department called upon industry to expand munitions production, and RTX has answered that call," he said. "This Tomahawk award increases our ability to equip the Joint Force, ensuring our Warfighters never face a fair fight."

What's Next

The Pentagon's push to rebuild the defense industrial base extends beyond any single weapons system. Administration officials have signaled that more multi-year production agreements are forthcoming as Washington seeks to shift from a peacetime procurement model to one capable of sustaining high-intensity warfare while simultaneously arming allies.

For RTX, the contract cements its position as the dominant supplier of sea-launched precision strike weapons and provides revenue visibility stretching into the early 2030s. The company operates Tomahawk production facilities in Tucson, Arizona, Huntsville, Alabama, and Andover, Massachusetts.
